title: Spinning with dog hair (chiengora)
subtitle: Preparing and spinning soft undercoat fibre from domestic dogs
excerpt: Dog undercoat (chiengora) can be spun into a warm, soft yarn with properties similar to angora. The key is using only the soft undercoat, not the coarse guard hairs. Double-coated breeds like Samoyed, Chow Chow, and Husky produce the best fibre; the yarn sheds less than raw angora.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from specialist guild workshop practice. Chiengora spinning is a well-documented niche fibre craft; the practical guidance here draws on the experience of spinners working with canine fibre in the UK and North America.

glossaryTerms.definition: Yarn spun from the soft undercoat of a domestic dog. The word blends the French word for dog (chien) with angora.
The coarse, water-repellent outer hair of a double-coated animal. Guard hairs do not spin well and must be removed before processing undercoat for yarn.
A spinning method where carded fibres are drafted with twist entering the zone, producing a lofty, air-filled yarn. Suitable for short-staple fibres like dog undercoat.

attrs.title: Allergen note
attrs.body: Dog fibre retains dander. Wash collected hair before spinning and work in a ventilated space if dander is a concern.

items.name: Brushed dog undercoat (clean and dry)
items.qty: as collected — at least 50 g for a useful spinning session

items.name: Merino roving for blending (optional but recommended)

content.text: Collect the undercoat from regular brushing sessions over several weeks or months. Double-coated breeds produce the most spinning fibre per brushing session. Wash the collected hair in warm water with a small amount of wool wash, without agitation, and let it dry fully before carding. Do not spin unwashed dog fibre: the dander and oils from the skin load the yarn and make it smell when wet.

Remove obvious guard hairs by hand before carding. Card the undercoat on the drum carder in thin, even passes. If blending with Merino, alternate thin layers of dog fibre and Merino on the drum until the batt is evenly mixed. A 50:50 blend is a practical starting point; more dog fibre increases the halo and warmth but can make the singles difficult to control. Card slowly to avoid tangling the short fibres.

Dog undercoat is short: the drafting zone must be kept very short (3 to 6 cm) or the fibres slip out of the draft zone before catching enough twist. Use a high ratio (14:1 to 18:1) and let the twist run into the batt frequently. The woollen draw works well here: open the front hand to let twist run ahead, then draft back. Keep the batt under slight tension to prevent it collapsing. Spin on a drop spindle if you find it difficult to control the short-staple draft at the wheel.

Ply two singles for a balanced 2-ply. Chiengora-blend yarn blooms noticeably after washing: the finished skein is loftier than the on-bobbin yarn. Wash in lukewarm water with minimal agitation. Dry flat. The yarn has a natural halo that increases with use and washing; this is normal and desirable in chiengora.

items.problem: The singles keep breaking every few centimetres
items.cause: The fibre is too short to hold together with the twist level being used, or guard hairs are causing weak spots at irregular intervals
items.fix: Increase twist substantially, shorten the drafting zone, and remove more guard hairs before carding. If the singles still break, add more Merino to the blend.

items.problem: The yarn smells of dog when it gets wet
items.cause: The collected hair was not washed sufficiently before spinning, leaving skin oils and dander in the fibre
items.fix: Wash the finished yarn in warm water with a small amount of wool wash, handling gently. Repeat if the smell persists. For future batches, wash the collected hair before carding.
